Title: How can we help?
Summary: First steps and common tasks.
Body:
Help for the current application

Select a category and topic on the left. Search covers titles and article text and accepts multiple words. Back and Forward follow visited articles. Ctrl+F focuses search, Alt+Left goes back and Escape closes the window.

Pictures are actual application windows using the current appearance and generated demo files only. Accounts, SMART readings and transfer progress are fictional. There are no numbered markers; click an image to open enlargement with a zoom slider.

Choose a workflow

  • Panels and tabs, preview and editor.
  • Copy, conflicts, deletion and archives.
  • Images, audio, metadata and CSV.
  • Search and duplicates, synchronization, analysis and SMART.
  • Settings, network, cloud and transaction history.

In the app and in a browser

Help is a separate package of HTML pages and images in the help folder beside the program. Press F1 in the app; Open in browser opens the current topic in your default browser. You can also open help/index.html directly without running the program or connecting to the internet. Help content is not embedded in the main EXE or interface language packs.

Title: Panels, tabs and selection
Summary: Source and destination panels, layout and selection.
Body:
Source and destination

The active panel has a strong blue outline. Click a panel or press Tab to change the source. F5 copies and F6 moves selected items to the opposite panel; check the destination before confirming.

Tabs and navigation

Below the drives is one blue-grey row, darker in the active panel. The white active tab joins the file area. Each tab has a borderless close cross, followed by + after the tabs, with parent and root buttons at the right. Ctrl+L or double-clicking the active tab opens address editing. Ctrl+T adds a tab; Ctrl+W, middle-click or the cross closes it. Closing the last tab can leave an empty panel; + opens a new location.

Unavailable drives and disconnected FTP/SFTP locations remain explicit unavailable tabs, which can still be closed. A connected remote tab first offers disconnect, close-tab-only or cancel. Disconnecting also affects other tabs sharing that connection.

Selection, filtering and columns

The current row and marked items are distinct. Marked items have a blue indicator on the left; adjacent marked rows share one bracket. Configure selection under Configuration → Files and operations. Typing in the list filters names; Escape clears the filter.

Right-click a column header to choose columns such as Extension or Attributes. Drag headers, or use the move-left/right commands, to reorder them. The sort arrow appears in the sorted column. Column widths and count fit the panel without a horizontal scrollbar. Choices are saved per panel and tab.

Drives and units

Drive buttons sit at the top; the right dropdown offers common folders rather than duplicate drive entries. Drive name, free space and capacity appear in the footer. Configure MB/GB, MiB/GiB or bytes and hidden/system-file visibility under Configuration → Panels.

Title: Preview, viewer and editor
Summary: F3, F4 and Ctrl+Q.
Body:
Quick preview

Ctrl+Q toggles preview in the opposite panel, F3 opens the viewer and F4 the editor. A single-panel layout can use bottom detail. Preview does not modify the file.

More and Details

Initially the preview shows the file and essential folder, size, date or dimension information. More with a downward arrow sits at the start of that row. It reveals a carousel of supported files; Less with an upward arrow hides it. The mouse wheel scrolls horizontally and document icons remain small. Details opens a separate window.

Choosing a carousel item also selects that file in the source panel while preserving marked items. Refreshing the folder therefore retains the chosen preview. Opening another source folder updates both preview and carousel; preview refresh does not replace a selected folder with a file.

Text and video

Automatic mode chooses a supported image, document, table or text view. Text uses editor typography, with encoding, wrapping and Text/Bin/Hex options. Supported videos show six frames from different times generated through FFmpeg. Clicking a frame or using Left/Right changes the enlarged frame; Play video is separate.

Remote preview may require consent and a cache download. Work can be cancelled and stale results from earlier selections are discarded. Escape closes the preview or details window.

Title: Internal editor and external applications
Summary: F4, syntax highlighting, YAML, JSON formatting and safe saves.
Body:
Current interface

The document name sits at the right of the Internal editor heading. New files use Windows CRLF; existing files retain their original form unless changed. Closing a modified document offers Save, Discard changes and Keep editing. Escape respects the unsaved-change check.

Current workflow

F2 or Ctrl+N opens a new unnamed text document in the internal editor. Its destination is the panel folder captured when it was created, even after navigating elsewhere. First Save asks only for a filename and extension in an application dialog. Replacing an existing file requires confirmation. Remote saving follows the connection capabilities. New documents default to UTF-8 without BOM and Windows CRLF; encoding and LF/CRLF remain selectable in the format bar. Existing documents preserve their format. The active filename appears at the right of the editor title. One document needs no tab strip; multiple documents keep their tabs. Unsaved changes offer Save, Discard changes and Keep editing. Syntax highlighting can be chosen before saving, including shell and RouterOS scripts. Shift+F6 renames a panel file; F2 no longer renames.

Opening and navigation

Select a local text or source file and press F4. The editor has its own window with document tabs; opening the same file again selects its existing tab. Settings include a switch for internal F4 text editing. Office documents and other non-text formats continue to use their external application.

Text and source code

Features include line numbers, highlighting by extension, indentation guides and JSON/YAML folding. Choose 2, 4 or 8 spaces; Tab inserts spaces. A new line inherits indentation and adds one level after a YAML colon or an opening brace/bracket. Check YAML nesting manually; the editor does not automatically rewrite the entire YAML document.

Ctrl+F opens search, Ctrl+H opens replacement of the next occurrence, and Ctrl+G goes to a line. Ctrl+Z/Ctrl+Y undo and redo edits. Showing spaces and tabs only changes their appearance.

Formatting and validation

JSON formatting preserves exact numeric spellings and key order, including large integers. Invalid JSON and duplicate keys stop formatting rather than being guessed or silently repaired. YAML validation streams parser events without expanding aliases. Validation checks syntax, not application-specific schema or semantics. XML validation prohibits DTD and external entities.

Encoding and saving

Normal saves retain the original encoding, BOM and line endings. UTF-8 and Unicode BOMs are recognized; non-UTF-8 text without a BOM falls back to Windows-1250. Explicit choices include UTF-8, UTF-8 BOM, UTF-16 LE, Windows-1250 and Windows-1252, plus CRLF/LF line endings. Characters unsupported by the selected encoding are not silently discarded.

The complete file is loaded, up to 16 MiB; binary data and links are rejected. Saving checks for changes made by another application and uses a temporary file. A conflict retains your document edits: use Save as, or decide which version to retain before reopening the original. Closing a modified document or the main window offers Save, Discard or Cancel.

Non-text files use the default registered Windows Open action. Executable scripts are sent to a text editor instead of being executed. FTP/SFTP and archive edits continue to use their existing working-copy and upload/commit workflow. See previews, network connections and archives.

F4 and Shift+F4

F4 opens supported text and source code in the internal editor. Excel, Word, PowerPoint, PDF, images, archives and other non-text types go directly to the default Windows Open action, such as Excel or a PDF reader, rather than a separate registered Edit action. Missing or broken associations open the Windows application chooser.

Shift+F4 immediately opens the external application for the current file; menus and the file context menu show this shortcut. Inside the internal editor it opens the current saved document externally. Editing scripts or executables passes them as data to a text editor instead of executing them.

External CSV and HTML editing

Shift+F4 and the external-edit command open CSV directly in Microsoft Excel. If Excel is missing or cannot be located, an error is shown rather than launching an unrelated program. HTML and HTM external editing explicitly uses Windows Notepad instead of a browser. Plain F4 still permits internal CSV and HTML editing. The external-edit toolbar icon has been removed; menus, the context command and Shift+F4 remain.

Choosing an application for an unassociated file

If an extension such as XLS has no default application, F4 and Shift+F4 show the Windows Open with dialog. Choose Excel or another suitable application. If Windows offers a permanent assignment, you can select it yourself; File Compass does not automatically overwrite associations. Broken registered applications use the same chooser. Cancelling simply closes it without an error.

Title: Copying files
Summary: F5, destination folder and transfer progress.
Body:
Check the original file before overwriting it. See conflict rules.

Current interface

More at the lower left expands blue-grey navigation; choosing a section replaces the main form. Overall and file progress are separate. Transfer details reveals further information. Run in background moves the task into the fixed-height lower strip. Pause and cancel controls at the right belong to that task.

Current workflow

Setup uses sidebar sections. Progress shows the whole job above a thinner blue current-file bar. Speed and further measurements are under Transfer details. Background docks the job in the bottom activity area; Detail restores it. Read/move errors offer Retry, Skip, Skip all and Cancel. Skipped move sources are retained. A symbolic link or junction is not necessarily a locked file; read the actual reported cause.

Check the original before overwriting. See collisions.

Step-by-step workflow

  1. Open the source in one panel and destination folder in the other. Select files and choose Copy / F5.
  2. Check the item count, destination and filter. The destination normally specifies a folder; use a destination including a new filename only for an appropriate single-file operation.
  3. Choose collision handling and preservation options. Enable SHA-256 verification when you need content checking; this reads additional data and takes more time.
  4. Copy starts the operation; Enqueue schedules it. During transfer, watch the current file, overall progress, speed and any prompts.

Understanding options

Preserve modification time retains the file timestamp; attributes preserve properties supported by the destination filesystem. Copying NTFS permissions requires a suitable filesystem and permissions; ordinary cloud storage does not implement identical semantics. Skipping hidden and system files can intentionally reduce the copied set. Copying empty folders preserves directory structures without files.

Interruption and errors

Cancel retains files already completed; it does not undo the entire batch. Resume only with the matching source and destination. History cannot reconstruct the original content of an overwritten file. See collisions, presets, safe undo and locked files.

Transfer-rate units

Rates use MiB/s: 1 MiB = 1,048,576 bytes. Decimal MB/s use 1,000,000 bytes and would display 4.8576% higher at the same throughput. The transfer rate includes read/write and inline SHA-256 processing; final flushing and optional verification also affect total elapsed time. Isolated screenshots cannot replace a complete-operation comparison under equal conditions.

Title: When a destination file already exists
Summary: Overwriting, skipping and applying a choice to more files.
Body:
Current interface

Existing and incoming files appear side by side. Check size, date and path; equal size and timestamps do not prove equal contents. Overwrite and Skip affect one conflict unless task-wide application is explicitly selected. More reveals additional rules.

Current workflow

Existing and incoming files are shown side by side. Overwrite, Skip and stopping the job remain directly accessible; rename, append and bulk rules use sidebar sections. Equal sizes and timestamps do not prove equal contents. A bulk collision policy lasts only for the current job.

Use content, not just names

A collision means the destination name already exists. Compare sizes, timestamps and, when appropriate, contents. A newer timestamp does not guarantee a better version: device clocks can differ and applications can preserve earlier timestamps.

  • Overwrite replaces destination content; back up the earlier version first if it matters.
  • Skip preserves the destination and continues with other items.
  • Renaming the output preserves both versions when the dialog offers that option.
  • Apply-to-all choices affect later collisions; use them only after confirming they suit the entire batch.

When uncertain, stop and use comparison or checksums. History is not a backup of overwritten content. Space or permission failures are not resolved by choosing a different collision policy.

Title: Creating and extracting archives
Summary: Compression, destination folder, passwords and multipart archives.
Body:
Current interface

Basic contains archive name, archiver, compression level and destination. Unsplit archive, No password and No SFX summaries open their corresponding sidebar pages. More expands the window to the left without narrowing the form. Splitting, file handling, security and SFX have separate sections.

Self-extracting archives (SFX)

Create archive → More → Tools → Self-extracting archive produces an EXE. 7z uses the bundled verified module. ZIP requires WinRAR.exe and Zip.SFX; RAR requires Default.SFX beside the configured RAR/WinRAR; ARJ requires ARJ32. TAR/GZ and LHA have no supported module here. Passwords are supported for 7z and ZIP. Keep a split-7z EXE and every .7z.001, .002… file together; other SFX formats are single volume. Creation does not run the EXE; move deletes sources only after verification.

External archiver licenses apply. ARJ Software SFX.TXT requires a separate distribution license for non-personal ARJ/ARJ32 SFX distribution. Existing SFX containers are read-only in archive browsing.

Current workflow

Destination, format and compression level are basic settings; additional options use sidebar sections. File preparation does not show misleading percentage bars; those appear during measurable processing. The selected level is mapped to the relevant archiver. Higher levels do not guarantee smaller output, especially for video, JPEG or already compressed data; uncompressed formats do not use a compression level. An unreadable or locked input offers retry, skip or stop instead of silently omitting it.

Create an archive

  1. Select source files and folders and choose Compress.
  2. Choose archive location, format and compression level. Select a format supported by the recipient, not merely a preferred extension.
  3. Avoid selecting an output archive as part of its own input tree. Read the offered action when the destination already exists.
  4. Create the archive and test that its contents can be read before deleting originals.

Browse and extract

An archive interior is a virtual location. Extract a file safely before using it with an ordinary application. Choose a destination and collision policy. Extracted contents may require much more space than the compressed archive; check destination capacity. A required password does not grant permission to overwrite unrelated files.

Read and write support differ by format. An external archiver may need configuration. For errors check format, damage, password, free space and tool availability. Cancellation does not certify a complete archive. See the archive reference and existing destinations.

Title: Network, NAS and remote connections
Summary: SMB, FTP, FTPS, SFTP and NFS.
Body:
Current interface

Connections has network and cloud tabs. In a profile editor, More at the lower left reveals Basic/Details navigation. Remote tabs can be closed with their cross even while disconnected; live connections distinguish closing the tab from disconnecting.

Choose the connection type

Network discovery helps locate devices but is not a complete service inventory. A computer may accept file transfers without announcing itself. Connect directly by known host name or address when discovery does not find it.

  • Windows and NAS shared folders: SMB, for example \\nas-demo\Shared.
  • SSH servers: SFTP, with host-key and user verification.
  • Other protocols must match the service and port actually enabled; the same IP does not imply the same login method.
  • Internet storage uses cloud connections rather than LAN computer discovery.

Saved connection and transfer

  1. Select protocol, address, port and authentication method.
  2. Connect and open a specific folder. Being able to list files does not establish write permission.
  3. Open the local source in the other panel and transfer a small test file first.
  4. After disconnection restore service availability before changing overwrite settings.

VPN transfers also depend on routing and DNS. Testing an IP address and a hostname are different checks. Missing discovery entries may reflect network segmentation or disabled announcements. See the connection reference.

Slow SMB reads

Folder creation and enumeration run outside the UI thread. A read that fails to respond within 15 seconds reports an error and permits refresh; a late older result cannot replace a newer listing. After a folder-creation timeout, refresh and check whether creation eventually succeeded before retrying. Pending system calls cannot always be cancelled immediately. Network entries use file-type icons so reading an individual remote file does not block the shared icon cache.

Title: Opening an SMB share
Summary: Direct UNC paths to a NAS or another computer.
Body:
Open a NAS or computer directly

Enter a UNC path such as \\nas-demo\Shared. The first part is the device name or IP, the second the actual share name, which may differ from its server-local disk or folder name. Direct access can work even when discovery does not list the device.

  1. Check device reachability on the LAN or VPN.
  2. Use an account and domain accepted by that server. A Windows account on another computer does not automatically have share access.
  3. After listing contents, test a small copy if write access is expected.
  4. For regular use save the path as a favorite or use supported network-drive mapping.

Windows may retain a connection to the same device under another account. Changing a password in one dialog does not necessarily end that system connection. Distinguish DNS failures, missing shares, authentication failures and subfolder permissions. See network connections.

Title: Connecting cloud storage
Summary: Google Drive, OneDrive, Dropbox and authorization.
Body:
Current interface

The picture contains fictional unsigned-in accounts. A selected profile does not mean an active connection. Sign-in availability depends on the provider and application configuration; respect the displayed Google OAuth notice.

Add and authorize an account

  1. Open cloud connection management, choose the service and assign a distinguishable connection name.
  2. Complete provider-specific authentication. Google Drive and OneDrive may require consent in a sign-in window.
  3. Confirm the intended account. Two accounts with the same provider are separate connections.
  4. Select the connection in a panel and wait for loading. When switching, check the active connection name and completion.

Google Drive, OneDrive and iCloud

Google may report application-verification or account restrictions; one successful account login does not prove universal public approval. OneDrive access varies with personal or organization account permissions. iCloud may require an additional Apple verification step and renewed authorization after session expiry. Supply only fields requested by the current provider dialog; field meanings are not universal across services.

Transfers and errors

Start with a small test file. Listings can lag and services can limit rate or requests. Renew invalid authorization instead of repeatedly overwriting files. Cloud quota exhaustion is not fixed by changing a local upload folder. Checksums and metadata may differ from local NTFS semantics. See the cloud reference.

Title: Finding files and duplicates
Summary: Name and content searches and duplicate files.
Body:
Current interface

More reveals sidebar navigation for additional criteria. File and duplicate searches are separate workflows. Before removing duplicates, inspect groups, paths and selected copies; equal names do not prove equal contents.

From names to contents

  1. Choose a root and whether to include subfolders. Wider scopes read more data.
  2. Enter a name mask such as *.jpg, then optional size or date limits.
  3. For content search enter text. PDF and DOCX search reads document text, not OCR from pictures.
  4. Run the search, inspect full paths and open the location or preview.

PDF/DOCX content search supports documents up to 64 MB with a 15-second processing limit. A scan without a text layer may not match visible words. A processing failure or limit is different from genuinely empty content.

Duplicates

Choose folders and wait for size comparison followed by full-content SHA-256. Duplicate files need not share names; equal names do not prove equal contents. Retain at least one copy in every group. Before deleting, check whether separate projects deliberately need their copies. Searching itself deletes nothing. See checksums and other tools.

Title: Comparing and synchronizing folders
Summary: Folder differences and transfer direction.
Body:
Current interface

One large arrow from the selected icon set sits between the folder cards. Clicking cycles rightward, bidirectional and leftward. Changing direction invalidates the plan; run Compare again. Bidirectional mode does not propagate deletion and disables mirroring. Synchronize applies the reviewed plan after confirmation.

Compare first, modify second

Open matching roots and start folder comparison or synchronization. Build the plan before applying it. Verify transfer directions and proposed deletions row by row: synchronization does not automatically mean preserving every file in both directions.

  1. Select roots, recursion and filters.
  2. Wait for comparison to finish; intermediate lists may be incomplete.
  3. Check left/right states, proposed directions and conflicts. Timestamp and size alone do not prove identical content.
  4. Remove unwanted steps or select a suitable conflict policy before confirming execution.
  5. Compare again afterward; another application can invalidate an earlier plan.

Keep backups before synchronization involving deletion. For browsing without changes, use linked panels. For content equality use checksums.

Title: Disk space analysis
Summary: Folder sizes, filters, exports and saved analyses.
Body:
Current interface

The analyzer uses simple sidebar tabs with icons. Results, scope/filters and progress/diagnostics share the main content area. Run in background creates a compact tile in the shared lower strip. The screenshot analyzes generated demo files only.

Current workflow

Opening the analyzer does not start a scan. Set Scope and filters, such as minimum size, then choose Start. Results reserve most space for files and the chart. Select the chart type above the chart; other parameters and diagnostics have separate sections. Background docks the window as a bottom activity tile with progress; Detail restores it. Overlapping roots are not counted twice.

Locate space usage

  1. Select a folder or disk and open disk space analysis.
  2. Wait for scanning. Intermediate totals are not final; inaccessible folders can limit results.
  3. Select a list or chart entry and drill into a folder. Size values use aligned columns rather than spacing guesses.
  4. Review largest files, types and ages using available filters. Open the actual location before deciding to delete.

File-size totals can differ from volume usage because of allocation, filesystem metadata, links, compression and permissions. An incomplete or empty result after access failures does not prove unused space. Charts represent size, not file importance.

Export a report when sharing findings and check whether it contains private names or paths. For device health see SMART; for identical copies see duplicates.

Treemap, size shares and multiple folders

By-folder maps show child folders and directly contained files. Up to 512 folders and 1024 direct files are displayed individually; remaining items are included in Other blocks. Selecting Other lists precisely those remaining items. Other grouping modes map the selected chart categories. Large expanded trees create primarily visible row containers and recycle them while scrolling.

Context actions and empty folders

Right-click the tree, map, legend or results for Open in panel, file preview, Copy path and Move to Recycle Bin when applicable. Aggregate blocks cannot accidentally delete a physical parent folder. Scan roots and drive roots are protected from this delete command.

Empty folders lists only genuinely empty, successfully read directories. Filtering files out does not make a nonempty directory eligible. Select multiple rows manually and use their context menu to move them to the Recycle Bin. Each folder is checked again before deletion. Network locations may not support recycling; Windows handles such failures.

Slow USB or network scans

The idle threshold sets how many seconds without progress trigger a warning; 0 disables the warning. This is not automatic termination. Stop requests cancellation and retains partial results. Retry scan first cancels existing work and restarts after it ends. A system read blocked inside a driver or network call must return before cancellation can finish; the application does not forcibly interrupt it. The last path and error help locate the problem.

Title: Language and appearance
Summary: Language changes without restart and theme settings.
Body:
One unified appearance

A blue-grey base, rounded white cards, pale groups and white fields form one consistent appearance. The outer shell uses subtle Windows Acrylic when supported and enabled, otherwise a solid background. White cards remain opaque. Folders use yellow Windows icons. Toolbar icons can be colored Fluent, Flat or Outline; Fluent is the default.

Where to find options

  • Appearance: language and separate interface/file-list fonts.
  • Icons: toolbar set, application icon and button/drive sizes. Sizes through 24 px use 2 px steps, followed by 4 px steps.
  • Panels: MB/GB, MiB/GiB or exact bytes, hidden and system files, automatic folder views and refresh.
  • Files and operations: list behavior, copying and the Recycle Bin preference.
  • Other sections: Archives, Viewers, View on startup, Network connections and Updates.

Units and saving

MB/GB uses decimal units (1 kB = 1,000 B); MiB/GiB uses binary units (1 KiB = 1,024 B). Bytes is the exact byte count. Hidden and system files have independent switches; a file with both attributes needs both enabled.

Apply saves settings and keeps the window open. Save saves and closes. Cancel discards subsequent unsaved edits; applied settings remain. Language changes take effect after saving without restarting. Profile management may save immediately as described in its interface.

Configuration keeps its left navigation visible. Other dialogs have More at the lower left to expand navigation; selecting a section replaces the main form. Less hides navigation while retaining values.

Title: Keyboard shortcuts
Summary: F1, F3, F4, F5, F6, F7, F8 and Ctrl+Q.
Body:
Current workflow

F2 / Ctrl+N: new text file. Shift+F6: rename. Ctrl+T / Ctrl+W: open / close a panel tab. F1: context help. Esc: close a secondary window through its normal safe close path; unsaved changes and running work may require confirmation. An open menu or list consumes the first Escape. Escape does not exit the main application.

Keys and context

Commands depend on the active panel and dialog. Enter opens the current list item but may execute the primary action in a confirmation dialog; read that action before pressing it. Esc normally closes a dialog or cancels its active operation. Keys in text fields may edit text instead of acting on files.

  • Tab switches panels when focus is not inside a dialog.
  • F1 opens context help for the current window.
  • F3 / F4 open viewer / editor.
  • F5 / F6 copy / move; F7 creates a folder, F8 deletes.
  • Ctrl+Q toggles quick preview; Ctrl+R refreshes contents manually.

Custom assignments can change command shortcuts. Check menu captions or custom shortcuts rather than assuming another file manager’s conventions.

Title: Troubleshooting
Summary: Missing network devices, denied access and interrupted transfers.
Body:
Troubleshooting sequence

  1. Record version, build and date from About. Distinguish a single-file failure from a whole-batch failure.
  2. Try a small demonstration file in a new local folder. Local success helps separate format problems from connection or permission failures.
  3. Check destination, free space, permissions, connectivity and other applications holding the file.
  4. For format failures inspect actual content, not just extension. For broken accents change preview encoding.
  5. For media failures reduce parallelism and try a common supported profile. Read the per-file queue error.

Useful bug reports

Describe steps, expected and actual results, location type and exact error. Remove private names, account addresses and credentials from screenshots; reproduce with a nonpersonal sample. Never send tokens, passwords or private keys. About can copy build diagnostics.

Specific guides: locks, CSV, authorization, audio and saving settings.

Title: Moving, renaming and creating folders
Summary: F6, Shift+F6 and F7.
Body:
Moving versus copying

Moving changes the original location; copying retains the source. Open source and destination, select items and use F6 / Move. Verify target path and item count. Moving across volumes or servers may require copying followed by source removal, so it is not necessarily as immediate as renaming within one folder.

Use F7 for a new folder and check which panel is active. Names must be valid on the target system and must not collide with existing items. After partial failures inspect each item; the whole batch is not necessarily rolled back. See batch rename and transaction history.

Title: Deleting files and folders
Summary: F8, confirmation and permissions.
Body:
Preferred action

Select items and choose Delete / F8. Configuration → Files and operations determines the main action: it sits on the right beside Cancel and Enter confirms it. The alternative sits separately on the left.

Move to Trash is blue. Delete permanently is red with white text and bypasses the Recycle Bin. The bottom Delete function key keeps its normal color. Shift can request permanent deletion. Check the location and selection before confirming.

Where recycling is unsupported, only permanent deletion can be confirmed and recycling is disabled. Recovery after permanent deletion is not guaranteed. Removing a connection profile does not delete its remote files.

Errors and background operation

Locked or unreadable items can offer retry, skip, skip all for the rest of the task, or cancel, depending on the operation. Skipped items are counted separately. Run in background places progress in the shared lower strip with controls for that specific task.

Title: Properties, attributes and timestamps
Summary: Alt+Enter and changing attributes.
Body:
Properties are not file content

Properties display or modify supported attributes and timestamps. Read-only may prevent writing; hidden/system attributes affect visibility according to panel settings. Such files are not automatically expendable.

  1. Select a file or intended group and open properties.
  2. Check the scope; a batch setting can affect many files.
  3. Distinguish creation, modification and access times. They are not automatically photo capture dates.
  4. Confirm, then check permissions and destination support if changes fail.

Changing a filesystem date does not necessarily alter EXIF or music tags. Use metadata tools for those. Clouds and other filesystems may support only some properties.

Title: Batch rename
Summary: Rules, numbering and name conflicts.
Body:
Safe workflow

  1. Select inputs and open batch rename. Verify ordering when using a counter.
  2. Build filename and extension patterns. Insert supported tokens from the menu; literal text remains in the output.
  3. Compare old and new names for every row. Check duplicates, empty results and characters invalid on the destination.
  4. Refresh preview after changing a pattern or files, then confirm.

Extensions influence application associations, but renaming is not format conversion. Renaming photo.png to photo.jpg does not create JPEG data; use image conversion. Filesystem creation and photo capture dates differ. See metadata for patterns and reverse writing, and history for limitations after subsequent changes.

Stable preview and recent values

Typing retains the last preview and updates existing row values instead of clearing the list. Start remains disabled until the new calculation succeeds, preventing stale previews from being applied. Arrow buttons beside the name, Find and Replace fields offer ten recent values for each field independently. History is saved when starting an operation and when closing the window, removes duplicates, and survives application restarts.

In the name field, press Alt alone or Alt+Down to open the placeholder menu. Clicking only positions the caret. The chosen token is inserted at the caret or replaces selected text. The same keyboard access applies to fields offering metadata tokens.

Title: Disk health / SMART
Summary: Health, temperature, wear and diagnostic export.
Body:
Current interface

The top tiles choose a disk; health, temperature and attributes belong to that device. Screenshot values are fictional, not readings from a user disk. Run in background creates a compact SMART tile.

Current workflow

Physical-drive cards distinguish HDD, SSD and NVMe when the type is available. USB bridges or unknown devices may not expose type or health; a missing value does not mean zero wear. Background docks the tool in the activity area and Detail restores it. A health status cannot guarantee that a drive will not fail.

Select the correct device

Each tile represents a physical disk with available information. Select it and check model, capacity and volume identifiers; several drive letters can belong to one disk. Temperature and summary health are quick indicators, not a complete diagnosis.

  1. Select a disk and wait for refresh.
  2. Review device information and SMART attributes. Raw-value meaning and units depend on manufacturer and device type.
  3. Compare trends over time. One value without context may not establish a failure.
  4. Copy data places text on the clipboard. Export saves an offered format, such as PNG or PDF, according to the dialog.

USB adapters, controllers, remote locations and permissions may limit SMART access. Missing data does not mean healthy or zero errors. Good status cannot guarantee against failure and is not a backup. For occupied file space use the separate disk space analyzer.

Title: Checksums
Summary: Creating and verifying file checksums.
Body:
Verify file contents

A checksum is calculated from all bytes read. Use the matching algorithm, such as SHA-256, to verify a copy or published file. Different algorithms produce different digests and cannot be compared to each other.

  1. Select files and start a supported algorithm.
  2. Wait for reading to finish; large files are limited by storage speed.
  3. Compare the complete digest with a trusted reference for the exact file version.
  4. When saving a list, use correct relative paths for future verification.

A matching checksum from the same untrusted source does not prove software origin or a digital signature. A read failure is not a valid completed digest. Copy verification can also be enabled directly in the operation dialog.

Title: Favorites and workspaces
Summary: Frequently used paths and panel layouts.
Body:
Current interface

Open favorites, folder history and tab management from application menus or a tab context menu. The row below drives contains tabs, +, parent and root navigation.

Favorites store frequently used paths; workspaces store related panel layouts and locations. They are not file backups or automatic service authorization.

  1. Open the required directories and arrange panels or tabs.
  2. Save a location or workspace with a clear name, such as Working project.
  3. When restoring it, check disks, VPN and connections. A reused drive letter can point to another device.
  4. Edit or remove obsolete saved locations; that does not delete destination files.

Use linked browsing to follow matching subfolders. Review personal paths and connection names before sharing configuration.

Title: Explorer, Command Prompt and PowerShell
Summary: Tools available in the Start menu.
Body:
External tools for the current location

Start groups Open in Explorer, Command Prompt and PowerShell. Activate the intended panel first. A local folder can serve as a working directory; clouds, archives and virtual locations may lack an ordinary process-accessible path.

  • Explorer opens the location in Windows when accessible.
  • Command Prompt opens the system command environment.
  • PowerShell opens the supported environment according to availability and settings.

Opening a shell itself transfers or deletes nothing. Commands entered afterward affect real data and may not belong to the application’s safe history. Check the displayed working directory before using relative paths.

Title: SFTP and server host keys
Summary: First connection and changed SSH keys.
Body:
Server identity differs from user authentication

SSH/SFTP identifies the server through its host key and authenticates you through an account or user key. On first connection compare the fingerprint with a value obtained from the administrator through another trusted route.

  1. Enter host, port, account and supported authentication method.
  2. Verify the host key. Acceptance records trust for later connections.
  3. After login check the remote folder and read/write permissions.
  4. Investigate changed stored keys: server reinstall, another device at the same IP or an unintended peer.

Blindly accepting changed keys defeats identity verification. SFTP access does not automatically grant permission to run arbitrary server commands. See network connections.

Title: Panels, columns and previews
Summary: Detailed workflows for the current interface with updated screenshots.
Body:
Panels, tabs and selection

Open this topic

Source and destination

The active panel has a strong blue outline. Click a panel or press Tab to change the source. F5 copies and F6 moves selected items to the opposite panel; check the destination before confirming.

Tabs and navigation

Below the drives is one blue-grey row, darker in the active panel. The white active tab joins the file area. Each tab has a borderless close cross, followed by + after the tabs, with parent and root buttons at the right. Ctrl+L or double-clicking the active tab opens address editing. Ctrl+T adds a tab; Ctrl+W, middle-click or the cross closes it. Closing the last tab can leave an empty panel; + opens a new location.

Unavailable drives and disconnected FTP/SFTP locations remain explicit unavailable tabs, which can still be closed. A connected remote tab first offers disconnect, close-tab-only or cancel. Disconnecting also affects other tabs sharing that connection.

Selection, filtering and columns

The current row and marked items are distinct. Marked items have a blue indicator on the left; adjacent marked rows share one bracket. Configure selection under Configuration → Files and operations. Typing in the list filters names; Escape clears the filter.

Right-click a column header to choose columns such as Extension or Attributes. Drag headers, or use the move-left/right commands, to reorder them. The sort arrow appears in the sorted column. Column widths and count fit the panel without a horizontal scrollbar. Choices are saved per panel and tab.

Drives and units

Drive buttons sit at the top; the right dropdown offers common folders rather than duplicate drive entries. Drive name, free space and capacity appear in the footer. Configure MB/GB, MiB/GiB or bytes and hidden/system-file visibility under Configuration → Panels.

Preview, viewer and editor

Open this topic

Quick preview

Ctrl+Q toggles preview in the opposite panel, F3 opens the viewer and F4 the editor. A single-panel layout can use bottom detail. Preview does not modify the file.

More and Details

Initially the preview shows the file and essential folder, size, date or dimension information. More with a downward arrow sits at the start of that row. It reveals a carousel of supported files; Less with an upward arrow hides it. The mouse wheel scrolls horizontally and document icons remain small. Details opens a separate window.

Choosing a carousel item also selects that file in the source panel while preserving marked items. Refreshing the folder therefore retains the chosen preview. Opening another source folder updates both preview and carousel; preview refresh does not replace a selected folder with a file.

Text and video

Automatic mode chooses a supported image, document, table or text view. Text uses editor typography, with encoding, wrapping and Text/Bin/Hex options. Supported videos show six frames from different times generated through FFmpeg. Clicking a frame or using Left/Right changes the enlarged frame; Play video is separate.

Remote preview may require consent and a cache download. Work can be cancelled and stale results from earlier selections are discarded. Escape closes the preview or details window.

Language and appearance

Open this topic

One unified appearance

A blue-grey base, rounded white cards, pale groups and white fields form one consistent appearance. The outer shell uses subtle Windows Acrylic when supported and enabled, otherwise a solid background. White cards remain opaque. Folders use yellow Windows icons. Toolbar icons can be colored Fluent, Flat or Outline; Fluent is the default.

Where to find options

  • Appearance: language and separate interface/file-list fonts.
  • Icons: toolbar set, application icon and button/drive sizes. Sizes through 24 px use 2 px steps, followed by 4 px steps.
  • Panels: MB/GB, MiB/GiB or exact bytes, hidden and system files, automatic folder views and refresh.
  • Files and operations: list behavior, copying and the Recycle Bin preference.
  • Other sections: Archives, Viewers, View on startup, Network connections and Updates.

Units and saving

MB/GB uses decimal units (1 kB = 1,000 B); MiB/GiB uses binary units (1 KiB = 1,024 B). Bytes is the exact byte count. Hidden and system files have independent switches; a file with both attributes needs both enabled.

Apply saves settings and keeps the window open. Save saves and closes. Cancel discards subsequent unsaved edits; applied settings remain. Language changes take effect after saving without restarting. Profile management may save immediately as described in its interface.

Configuration keeps its left navigation visible. Other dialogs have More at the lower left to expand navigation; selecting a section replaces the main form. Less hides navigation while retaining values.

Title: Copying, recovery and operations
Summary: Detailed workflows for the current interface with updated screenshots.
Body:
Copying files

Open this topic

Check the original file before overwriting it. See conflict rules.

Current interface

More at the lower left expands blue-grey navigation; choosing a section replaces the main form. Overall and file progress are separate. Transfer details reveals further information. Run in background moves the task into the fixed-height lower strip. Pause and cancel controls at the right belong to that task.

Current workflow

Setup uses sidebar sections. Progress shows the whole job above a thinner blue current-file bar. Speed and further measurements are under Transfer details. Background docks the job in the bottom activity area; Detail restores it. Read/move errors offer Retry, Skip, Skip all and Cancel. Skipped move sources are retained. A symbolic link or junction is not necessarily a locked file; read the actual reported cause.

Check the original before overwriting. See collisions.

Step-by-step workflow

  1. Open the source in one panel and destination folder in the other. Select files and choose Copy / F5.
  2. Check the item count, destination and filter. The destination normally specifies a folder; use a destination including a new filename only for an appropriate single-file operation.
  3. Choose collision handling and preservation options. Enable SHA-256 verification when you need content checking; this reads additional data and takes more time.
  4. Copy starts the operation; Enqueue schedules it. During transfer, watch the current file, overall progress, speed and any prompts.

Understanding options

Preserve modification time retains the file timestamp; attributes preserve properties supported by the destination filesystem. Copying NTFS permissions requires a suitable filesystem and permissions; ordinary cloud storage does not implement identical semantics. Skipping hidden and system files can intentionally reduce the copied set. Copying empty folders preserves directory structures without files.

Interruption and errors

Cancel retains files already completed; it does not undo the entire batch. Resume only with the matching source and destination. History cannot reconstruct the original content of an overwritten file. See collisions, presets, safe undo and locked files.

Transfer-rate units

Rates use MiB/s: 1 MiB = 1,048,576 bytes. Decimal MB/s use 1,000,000 bytes and would display 4.8576% higher at the same throughput. The transfer rate includes read/write and inline SHA-256 processing; final flushing and optional verification also affect total elapsed time. Isolated screenshots cannot replace a complete-operation comparison under equal conditions.

When a destination file already exists

Open this topic

Current interface

Existing and incoming files appear side by side. Check size, date and path; equal size and timestamps do not prove equal contents. Overwrite and Skip affect one conflict unless task-wide application is explicitly selected. More reveals additional rules.

Current workflow

Existing and incoming files are shown side by side. Overwrite, Skip and stopping the job remain directly accessible; rename, append and bulk rules use sidebar sections. Equal sizes and timestamps do not prove equal contents. A bulk collision policy lasts only for the current job.

Use content, not just names

A collision means the destination name already exists. Compare sizes, timestamps and, when appropriate, contents. A newer timestamp does not guarantee a better version: device clocks can differ and applications can preserve earlier timestamps.

  • Overwrite replaces destination content; back up the earlier version first if it matters.
  • Skip preserves the destination and continues with other items.
  • Renaming the output preserves both versions when the dialog offers that option.
  • Apply-to-all choices affect later collisions; use them only after confirming they suit the entire batch.

When uncertain, stop and use comparison or checksums. History is not a backup of overwritten content. Space or permission failures are not resolved by choosing a different collision policy.

Moving, renaming and creating folders

Open this topic

Moving versus copying

Moving changes the original location; copying retains the source. Open source and destination, select items and use F6 / Move. Verify target path and item count. Moving across volumes or servers may require copying followed by source removal, so it is not necessarily as immediate as renaming within one folder.

Use F7 for a new folder and check which panel is active. Names must be valid on the target system and must not collide with existing items. After partial failures inspect each item; the whole batch is not necessarily rolled back. See batch rename and transaction history.

Deleting files and folders

Open this topic

Preferred action

Select items and choose Delete / F8. Configuration → Files and operations determines the main action: it sits on the right beside Cancel and Enter confirms it. The alternative sits separately on the left.

Move to Trash is blue. Delete permanently is red with white text and bypasses the Recycle Bin. The bottom Delete function key keeps its normal color. Shift can request permanent deletion. Check the location and selection before confirming.

Where recycling is unsupported, only permanent deletion can be confirmed and recycling is disabled. Recovery after permanent deletion is not guaranteed. Removing a connection profile does not delete its remote files.

Errors and background operation

Locked or unreadable items can offer retry, skip, skip all for the rest of the task, or cancel, depending on the operation. Skipped items are counted separately. Run in background places progress in the shared lower strip with controls for that specific task.

Transaction history and safe undo

Open this topic

History and undo

The curved toolbar arrow opens transaction history. Rows explain available, partially available and irreversible operations. Review details before undoing; a partial operation offers only available steps.

Copy, move or rename operations can have verified undo receipts. Identity and contents are rechecked; later edits, replacement files or unrelated folder contents may prevent undo. Overwriting and permanent deletion are not backups. Receipts are available in the current session; a persisted record alone does not guarantee undo after restarting.

Clear history

Transaction history and operation history offer Clear history with confirmation. It removes completed records and their undo receipts without changing actual files. Running and queued tasks remain. The control can be disabled during work or availability checks. Clearing is persisted, so removed records do not return after reloading.

Log

Operation history offers details, log export and, where available, retry or resume for interrupted tasks. Check paths and filenames before sharing a log.

Title: Search, metadata and tools
Summary: Detailed workflows for the current interface with updated screenshots.
Body:
Finding files and duplicates

Open this topic

Current interface

More reveals sidebar navigation for additional criteria. File and duplicate searches are separate workflows. Before removing duplicates, inspect groups, paths and selected copies; equal names do not prove equal contents.

From names to contents

  1. Choose a root and whether to include subfolders. Wider scopes read more data.
  2. Enter a name mask such as *.jpg, then optional size or date limits.
  3. For content search enter text. PDF and DOCX search reads document text, not OCR from pictures.
  4. Run the search, inspect full paths and open the location or preview.

PDF/DOCX content search supports documents up to 64 MB with a 15-second processing limit. A scan without a text layer may not match visible words. A processing failure or limit is different from genuinely empty content.

Duplicates

Choose folders and wait for size comparison followed by full-content SHA-256. Duplicate files need not share names; equal names do not prove equal contents. Retain at least one copy in every group. Before deleting, check whether separate projects deliberately need their copies. Searching itself deletes nothing. See checksums and other tools.

Batch rename

Open this topic

Safe workflow

  1. Select inputs and open batch rename. Verify ordering when using a counter.
  2. Build filename and extension patterns. Insert supported tokens from the menu; literal text remains in the output.
  3. Compare old and new names for every row. Check duplicates, empty results and characters invalid on the destination.
  4. Refresh preview after changing a pattern or files, then confirm.

Extensions influence application associations, but renaming is not format conversion. Renaming photo.png to photo.jpg does not create JPEG data; use image conversion. Filesystem creation and photo capture dates differ. See metadata for patterns and reverse writing, and history for limitations after subsequent changes.

Stable preview and recent values

Typing retains the last preview and updates existing row values instead of clearing the list. Start remains disabled until the new calculation succeeds, preventing stale previews from being applied. Arrow buttons beside the name, Find and Replace fields offer ten recent values for each field independently. History is saved when starting an operation and when closing the window, removes duplicates, and survives application restarts.

In the name field, press Alt alone or Alt+Down to open the placeholder menu. Clicking only positions the caret. The chosen token is inserted at the caret or replaces selected text. The same keyboard access applies to fields offering metadata tokens.

Checksums

Open this topic

Verify file contents

A checksum is calculated from all bytes read. Use the matching algorithm, such as SHA-256, to verify a copy or published file. Different algorithms produce different digests and cannot be compared to each other.

  1. Select files and start a supported algorithm.
  2. Wait for reading to finish; large files are limited by storage speed.
  3. Compare the complete digest with a trusted reference for the exact file version.
  4. When saving a list, use correct relative paths for future verification.

A matching checksum from the same untrusted source does not prove software origin or a digital signature. A read failure is not a valid completed digest. Copy verification can also be enabled directly in the operation dialog.

Disk space analysis

Open this topic

Current interface

The analyzer uses simple sidebar tabs with icons. Results, scope/filters and progress/diagnostics share the main content area. Run in background creates a compact tile in the shared lower strip. The screenshot analyzes generated demo files only.

Current workflow

Opening the analyzer does not start a scan. Set Scope and filters, such as minimum size, then choose Start. Results reserve most space for files and the chart. Select the chart type above the chart; other parameters and diagnostics have separate sections. Background docks the window as a bottom activity tile with progress; Detail restores it. Overlapping roots are not counted twice.

Locate space usage

  1. Select a folder or disk and open disk space analysis.
  2. Wait for scanning. Intermediate totals are not final; inaccessible folders can limit results.
  3. Select a list or chart entry and drill into a folder. Size values use aligned columns rather than spacing guesses.
  4. Review largest files, types and ages using available filters. Open the actual location before deciding to delete.

File-size totals can differ from volume usage because of allocation, filesystem metadata, links, compression and permissions. An incomplete or empty result after access failures does not prove unused space. Charts represent size, not file importance.

Export a report when sharing findings and check whether it contains private names or paths. For device health see SMART; for identical copies see duplicates.

Treemap, size shares and multiple folders

By-folder maps show child folders and directly contained files. Up to 512 folders and 1024 direct files are displayed individually; remaining items are included in Other blocks. Selecting Other lists precisely those remaining items. Other grouping modes map the selected chart categories. Large expanded trees create primarily visible row containers and recycle them while scrolling.

Context actions and empty folders

Right-click the tree, map, legend or results for Open in panel, file preview, Copy path and Move to Recycle Bin when applicable. Aggregate blocks cannot accidentally delete a physical parent folder. Scan roots and drive roots are protected from this delete command.

Empty folders lists only genuinely empty, successfully read directories. Filtering files out does not make a nonempty directory eligible. Select multiple rows manually and use their context menu to move them to the Recycle Bin. Each folder is checked again before deletion. Network locations may not support recycling; Windows handles such failures.

Slow USB or network scans

The idle threshold sets how many seconds without progress trigger a warning; 0 disables the warning. This is not automatic termination. Stop requests cancellation and retains partial results. Retry scan first cancels existing work and restarts after it ends. A system read blocked inside a driver or network call must return before cancellation can finish; the application does not forcibly interrupt it. The last path and error help locate the problem.

Disk health / SMART

Open this topic

Current interface

The top tiles choose a disk; health, temperature and attributes belong to that device. Screenshot values are fictional, not readings from a user disk. Run in background creates a compact SMART tile.

Current workflow

Physical-drive cards distinguish HDD, SSD and NVMe when the type is available. USB bridges or unknown devices may not expose type or health; a missing value does not mean zero wear. Background docks the tool in the activity area and Detail restores it. A health status cannot guarantee that a drive will not fail.

Select the correct device

Each tile represents a physical disk with available information. Select it and check model, capacity and volume identifiers; several drive letters can belong to one disk. Temperature and summary health are quick indicators, not a complete diagnosis.

  1. Select a disk and wait for refresh.
  2. Review device information and SMART attributes. Raw-value meaning and units depend on manufacturer and device type.
  3. Compare trends over time. One value without context may not establish a failure.
  4. Copy data places text on the clipboard. Export saves an offered format, such as PNG or PDF, according to the dialog.

USB adapters, controllers, remote locations and permissions may limit SMART access. Missing data does not mean healthy or zero errors. Good status cannot guarantee against failure and is not a backup. For occupied file space use the separate disk space analyzer.

Title: Archives and archivers
Summary: Detailed workflows for the current interface with updated screenshots.
Body:
Creating and extracting archives

Open this topic

Current interface

Basic contains archive name, archiver, compression level and destination. Unsplit archive, No password and No SFX summaries open their corresponding sidebar pages. More expands the window to the left without narrowing the form. Splitting, file handling, security and SFX have separate sections.

Self-extracting archives (SFX)

Create archive → More → Tools → Self-extracting archive produces an EXE. 7z uses the bundled verified module. ZIP requires WinRAR.exe and Zip.SFX; RAR requires Default.SFX beside the configured RAR/WinRAR; ARJ requires ARJ32. TAR/GZ and LHA have no supported module here. Passwords are supported for 7z and ZIP. Keep a split-7z EXE and every .7z.001, .002… file together; other SFX formats are single volume. Creation does not run the EXE; move deletes sources only after verification.

External archiver licenses apply. ARJ Software SFX.TXT requires a separate distribution license for non-personal ARJ/ARJ32 SFX distribution. Existing SFX containers are read-only in archive browsing.

Current workflow

Destination, format and compression level are basic settings; additional options use sidebar sections. File preparation does not show misleading percentage bars; those appear during measurable processing. The selected level is mapped to the relevant archiver. Higher levels do not guarantee smaller output, especially for video, JPEG or already compressed data; uncompressed formats do not use a compression level. An unreadable or locked input offers retry, skip or stop instead of silently omitting it.

Create an archive

  1. Select source files and folders and choose Compress.
  2. Choose archive location, format and compression level. Select a format supported by the recipient, not merely a preferred extension.
  3. Avoid selecting an output archive as part of its own input tree. Read the offered action when the destination already exists.
  4. Create the archive and test that its contents can be read before deleting originals.

Browse and extract

An archive interior is a virtual location. Extract a file safely before using it with an ordinary application. Choose a destination and collision policy. Extracted contents may require much more space than the compressed archive; check destination capacity. A required password does not grant permission to overwrite unrelated files.

Read and write support differ by format. An external archiver may need configuration. For errors check format, damage, password, free space and tool availability. Cancellation does not certify a complete archive. See the archive reference and existing destinations.

Title: Cloud accounts, authorization and transfers
Summary: Detailed workflows for the current interface with updated screenshots.
Body:
Connecting cloud storage

Open this topic

Current interface

The picture contains fictional unsigned-in accounts. A selected profile does not mean an active connection. Sign-in availability depends on the provider and application configuration; respect the displayed Google OAuth notice.

Add and authorize an account

  1. Open cloud connection management, choose the service and assign a distinguishable connection name.
  2. Complete provider-specific authentication. Google Drive and OneDrive may require consent in a sign-in window.
  3. Confirm the intended account. Two accounts with the same provider are separate connections.
  4. Select the connection in a panel and wait for loading. When switching, check the active connection name and completion.

Google Drive, OneDrive and iCloud

Google may report application-verification or account restrictions; one successful account login does not prove universal public approval. OneDrive access varies with personal or organization account permissions. iCloud may require an additional Apple verification step and renewed authorization after session expiry. Supply only fields requested by the current provider dialog; field meanings are not universal across services.

Transfers and errors

Start with a small test file. Listings can lag and services can limit rate or requests. Renew invalid authorization instead of repeatedly overwriting files. Cloud quota exhaustion is not fixed by changing a local upload folder. Checksums and metadata may differ from local NTFS semantics. See the cloud reference.

Network, NAS and remote connections

Open this topic

Current interface

Connections has network and cloud tabs. In a profile editor, More at the lower left reveals Basic/Details navigation. Remote tabs can be closed with their cross even while disconnected; live connections distinguish closing the tab from disconnecting.

Choose the connection type

Network discovery helps locate devices but is not a complete service inventory. A computer may accept file transfers without announcing itself. Connect directly by known host name or address when discovery does not find it.

  • Windows and NAS shared folders: SMB, for example \\nas-demo\Shared.
  • SSH servers: SFTP, with host-key and user verification.
  • Other protocols must match the service and port actually enabled; the same IP does not imply the same login method.
  • Internet storage uses cloud connections rather than LAN computer discovery.

Saved connection and transfer

  1. Select protocol, address, port and authentication method.
  2. Connect and open a specific folder. Being able to list files does not establish write permission.
  3. Open the local source in the other panel and transfer a small test file first.
  4. After disconnection restore service availability before changing overwrite settings.

VPN transfers also depend on routing and DNS. Testing an IP address and a hostname are different checks. Missing discovery entries may reflect network segmentation or disabled announcements. See the connection reference.

Slow SMB reads

Folder creation and enumeration run outside the UI thread. A read that fails to respond within 15 seconds reports an error and permits refresh; a late older result cannot replace a newer listing. After a folder-creation timeout, refresh and check whether creation eventually succeeded before retrying. Pending system calls cannot always be cancelled immediately. Network entries use file-type icons so reading an individual remote file does not block the shared icon cache.

SFTP and server host keys

Open this topic

Server identity differs from user authentication

SSH/SFTP identifies the server through its host key and authenticates you through an account or user key. On first connection compare the fingerprint with a value obtained from the administrator through another trusted route.

  1. Enter host, port, account and supported authentication method.
  2. Verify the host key. Acceptance records trust for later connections.
  3. After login check the remote folder and read/write permissions.
  4. Investigate changed stored keys: server reinstall, another device at the same IP or an unintended peer.

Blindly accepting changed keys defeats identity verification. SFTP access does not automatically grant permission to run arbitrary server commands. See network connections.
